content:
The well-used work board at Bass Phillip Estate in the Gippsland Region of Victoria, Australia easily earns the label of palimpsest, a surface (originally a skin or parchment) which bears the traces of much previous writing and erasing. One of Australia’s legendary Pinot Noir estates, Bass Philip was purchased in recent years by investors led by Burgundy legend Jean-Marie Fourrier, but still operates with the same facilities and equipment long used by its idiosyncratic founder Phillip Jones.

title: Why South Africa Is the Most Exciting Wine Region on the Planet, Part II
summary:

The post Why South Africa Is the Most Exciting Wine Region on the Planet, Part II appeared first on Vinography.
content:
This is Part II of a lengthy piece on South African wine. Read Part I here.

In Part I, I used the anarchic camaraderie of the Zoo Cru to illustrate something fundamental about South African wine: its unusual culture of collaboration. But collegiality alone cannot explain the country’s astonishing momentum. South Africa’s excitement comes from a convergence of ancient landscapes, old vineyards, stylistic relevance, brilliant hospitality, and a depth of winemaking talent that few regions can match.

Phenomenal Raw Materials

Those of us in the wine business often like to point out that the places where wine grows around the world are beautiful, which is true for the most part. But few bits of wine country can hold a candle to the sweeping beauty of South Africa.

Spectacular mountain vistas plunge toward the sea; craggy windswept highlands transform to lush protea-filled forests hosting troops of baboons; remote moonlike rocky plateaus can feel otherworldly. Some corners of the country feel nearly tropical while, elsewhere, stretches of bounteous farmland offer idyllic pastoral views.

The landscape of South Africa demands your attention and rewards your gaze at every turn. Anyone who comes over the pass into the valley of Franschhoek and fails to have their breath taken away should probably just be put out of their own misery.

Geologically speaking, a trip through the South African landscape represents an excursion into deep time. The country harbors some of the globe’s oldest, well-preserved exposed rocks and layers formed by sedimentary and volcanic activity, dating to more than 3.22 billion years ago.

Unlike some younger landscapes shaped primarily by tectonic uplift and volcanic eruptions, South Africa’s peaks, valleys, plains, and plateaus have largely been carved by billions of years of wind and water, punctuated by occasional cataclysms such as continental collisions and asteroid impacts. That geological complexity has left the Cape with an extraordinary mosaic of soils capable of supporting a wide range of grapevines.

South Africa’s wine country sits within a broadly Mediterranean climate, with warm, dry summers and cool, wet winters. But conditions vary tremendously throughout the Cape. Much of the Western Cape is cooled by the Atlantic Ocean and its icy Benguela Current, which generates fog and sends moisture-laden breezes into coastal vineyards during the growing season.

The country’s jagged mountains add even more variation. Elevation, slope, aspect, and distance from the sea can produce distinctly different mesoclimates within very short distances. Rainfall also varies dramatically, generally diminishing as you move north and inland, from relatively lush coastal and mountain sites to arid places where the survival of dry-farmed vineyards can seem almost miraculous. These climatic differences allow South Africa to ripen an enormous range of grape varieties. They have also helped produce an equally remarkable diversity of native plant life.

On top of South Africa’s stones and soil sits one of the world’s most diverse ecological zones, the Cape Floristic Region, sometimes known as the Cape Floral Kingdom. A combination of Mediterranean climate, infertile soils, recurrent wildfires, and wildly varying landscapes has contributed to the evolutionary isolation of the region. The resulting environment encouraged millions of years of what biologists call speciation, or the proliferation of new and different species from existing ones.

The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of six floral kingdoms around the world, but the most diverse of them relative to its size. It hosts approximately 9,000 different plant species, of which more than 6,200 are found nowhere else on Earth. The characteristic vegetation of the kingdom is known as fynbos, a mix of dazzling floral plants such as protea and many other evergreen flowering shrubs, heaths, grasses, wildflowers, and succulents.

Walking through fynbos offers an experience as aromatic as it is visual. Like the characteristic garrigue of southeastern France, fynbos offers rich and unique smells including rooibos (which many people know from its popularity as a tisane), as well as other resinous and herbal aromas. Just as in Provence, these aromas can show up in the wines, sometimes hauntingly.

A Treasure Hiding in Plain Sight

One of the species that doesn’t naturally belong in this Cape Floral ecosystem is the wine grapevine, but Vitis vinifera has seemingly been quite comfortable in the nutrient-poor, rocky soils of the Cape since it arrived in 1655, carried and planted by Dutch settler Jan van Riebeeck.

His success in making the first wines in South Africa in 1659 encouraged farmers to plant vines wherever they saw fit to do so, and a particular set of economic and market realities ensured many of them stayed there.

South Africa, like some other sections of wine country around the world, possesses an incredible bounty of old vines, for many of the same reasons that Lodi in California still hosts a plethora of ancient Zinfandel.

The KWV Cooperative, soon after its launch in 1918, became the dominant force in the South African wine industry, eventually controlling the vast majority of its production with strict rules for growers. As a reliable customer to thousands of individual grape farmers throughout the country, KWV was counted on to purchase grapes for many decades. This steady, guaranteed income encouraged farmers to leave their vines in the ground and forgo the effort and expense of replanting or replacing them with other crops.

Later in the 20th century, when the wine market fell on hard times, it became simply too expensive to consider replanting them, or even ripping them out, so thousands of acres of mature vines, including precious scattered parcels approaching or exceeding a century in age, remained planted and in many cases producing. Today these vineyards are sought-after gems, prized by winemakers who understand the treasure that was hiding in plain sight.

South Africa owes its newfound appreciation for these old-vine resources largely to one person: Rosa Kruger. Kruger made early career stops in journalism and law before moving into agricultural management and viticulture in the late 1990s. In the early 2000s, inspired by visits to other regions around the world with old vines, she began to wonder what South Africa might have in the way of old vines. This led to years of driving around the country, discovering and documenting the country’s old vineyards.

In 2016, she formally established the Old Vine Project, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and ensuring the value of South Africa’s old-vine vineyards. What she has accomplished under the banner of this organization in a mere decade is astonishing.

Using planting records verified by South African Wine Industry Information and Systems (SAWIS), the Old Vine Project introduced its Certified Heritage Vineyard seal in 2018 for vineyards at least 35 years old. This first-of-its-kind program is designed to generate more revenue for the farmers of these old vines, and it’s working. Research suggests that South African consumers place a measurable premium on wines identified as coming from old vines.

The Old Vine Project has elevated and foregrounded the conversation about old vineyards and their value across culture, genetics, agronomy, history, and wine quality, as well as inspired many other old-vine initiatives around the world, including the Old Vine Registry.

Many Routes to Delicious

A great wine region offers more than compelling bottles. It also rewards wine lovers who make the journey to stand among its vines.

Wine tourism in South Africa has improved significantly in the past 20 years and now offers an impressive array of experiences for serious wine lovers as well as the merely wine-inclined world traveler. The Western Cape boasts more than 20 distinct wine regions, many with strong regional identities and well-established Wine Routes.

The Cape Town wine region puts wineries within easy reach of the cosmopolitan and lively city of the same name, making winery stops possible via taxi or rideshare, even down to rugged Cape Point, where crisp Sauvignon Blancs can be consumed oceanside with fresh seafood. Nearby Constantia offers beautiful historic estates with ocean views, while Stellenbosch surrounds a small town packed with restaurants, shops, and bars. The epicenter of Cabernet Sauvignon production in South Africa, Stellenbosch makes historic estates such as Kanonkop and Meerlust key pilgrimage stops for Cab lovers.

With a car, wine lovers can go farther afield. The cooler-climate Elgin Valley and Bot River regions make excellent Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, and increasingly interesting Rhône varieties. Farther along the coast, the windswept and craggy Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and Walker Bay countryside offer excellent Pinot Noir, stunning coastline, and some of the most consistent whale watching anywhere in the world.

Franschhoek offers stunning mountain landscapes, excellent wines, boutique hotels, and good restaurants. What the Swartland lacks in tourist infrastructure, it makes up for in sweeping vistas and spectacular wines, many of which come from old vines. More remote regions require slightly more planning, but readily welcome visitors, and increasing numbers of wineries offer guest accommodations, some of them quite luxurious.

South African wineries also offer some of the most impressive dining opportunities in the country. When the Michelin Guide gets to South Africa—not really a question of if, but when—mark my words, there will be more starred restaurants at wineries than in Cape Town itself. Many wineries now offer full-service dining, and a few of those kitchens are truly world-class.

There’s great food all over South Africa, with a strong focus on local sourcing, indigenous ingredients, and even foraging. Ocean bounty, wild game, excellent beef, and seasonal produce give local chefs plenty to work with. I have come to adore the country’s culinary variety, from casual braais to haute cuisine.

Beyond wine and food, South Africa offers mountain biking, surfing, hiking, paragliding, wildlife safaris, and the cosmopolitan vibrance of Cape Town. Combine all that with the quality and distinctiveness of the country’s wines, and South Africa easily vaults into the top tier of wine destinations around the world.

Beauty, hospitality, and a compelling travel experience alone do not make a great wine culture. Ultimately, the argument for South Africa being the world’s most exciting wine country rests on what ends up in the glass.

Fine Wines for Today’s Drinkers

Among the sommeliers, merchants, and engaged drinkers who shape conversations about wines over $25, the past 10 years have seen a growing appetite for freshness, moderate alcohol, less conspicuous oak, less-familiar grape varieties, and wines with strong regional identities.

South Africa’s current wine scene seems shockingly tailor-made for this moment. A whole generation of winemakers, informed by the pioneers of the Swartland Revolution, have adopted a lower-intervention approach to winemaking that, in addition to making thrilling wines, does an incredible job of showcasing South Africa’s varied terroir. The relative absence of new-oak signatures, combined with picking dates that preserve acidity and moderate ripeness, allows these wines to foreground site over cellar technique.

These winemakers have fully embraced the old-vine legacy of their homeland and now go to great lengths to ferret out patches of old vines and heritage grape varieties. South Africa is now making world-class Syrah, Cinsault, Grenache, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Palomino, Colombard, and of course, Chenin Blanc, in addition to stalwarts such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and the uniquely local grape Pinotage. After years of a few producers making separate bottlings with the rosy-colored fruit that some of their Semillon vines occasionally produced, in 2026 the government recognized Semillon Gris as a legal variety, paving the way for another idiosyncratic South African winegrape rarely found elsewhere in the world.

When it comes to bubbles, South Africa has spent decades perfecting Cap Classique, its traditional-method sparkling wine. Made with the traditional Champagne grapes (Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Pinot Meunier) much of the time, the wine can also be made with Chenin Blanc, offering a particularly delicious take on the region’s signature white grape. Some Cap Classique producers have taken to very long lees aging, much like prestige Champagnes, and the results can be electrifying.

Pinotage represents perhaps the most stubbornly “local” grape variety found in South Africa. Developed in Stellenbosch in 1925 as a cross between Cinsault and Pinot Noir, it has long been considered the country’s signature red grape, but has struggled to win over many consumers. However, a newer approach to winemaking and site selection shows great promise, as I wrote about in my article Pinotage is Dead, Long Live Pinotage! earlier this year.

A discussion of South African wine styles would not be complete without the late-harvest sweet wines that made the country famous in the 18th and 19th centuries. Often made from Muscat, historically known as Hanepoot, these unfortified wines were once in high demand around the world. Today, wines such as Vin de Constance have revived the tradition in small but delicious quantities, combining vivid sweetness with enough acidity to stand alongside the world’s legendary dessert wines.

A New Homeland for Chenin

Chenin first came to South Africa in Jan van Riebeeck’s initial importation of grapevines in 1655 and was known locally as Steen for more than 300 years until 1963, when it was identified conclusively as Chenin Blanc.

Interestingly, some of the Chenin Blanc plant material that has been grown in South Africa for three centuries no longer exists in the Loire Valley. What’s more, recent research suggests that centuries of propagation under South African conditions have produced measurable epigenetic differences from Loire material, adding another dimension to the Cape’s distinctive expression of the grape.

I believe South Africa now rivals or even exceeds the grape’s homeland in the Loire Valley in producing extremely high-quality bottlings of this grape. That’s a bold statement, to be sure, but I confidently stand behind it. There are a few superstar producers of Chenin Blanc in the Loire that are unassailable, of course, but the Loire also makes plenty of mediocre Chenin. South Africa, on the other hand, can be distinguished not only by the heights of its greatest Chenins but also by the sheer breadth of excellence beneath them.

Talent at an Exceptional Scale

One of the most impressive things about South African wine right now is the sheer number of world-class independent wine producers making wine at the top of their game. In most wine regions around the world, only a small new wave of producers, often from a younger generation, defines the cutting edge of winemaking with exceptional wines. Think Chacra in Argentina; Comando G in Spain; or Kusuda in New Zealand. You get the idea.

South Africa doesn’t just have a handful of these producers; it has many dozens of such independent producers and labels in addition to the members of the Zoo Cru that I highlighted in Part I of this narrative. These are producers whose portfolios I can taste through, and after eight, ten, even fifteen wines, I haven’t encountered a single disappointing wine.

This isn’t normal for a region still considered up-and-coming in the world, especially not one that has only been developing in the modern sense since the end of apartheid in 1994. What South Africa has accomplished in the last three decades simply blows my mind.

Eben Sadie and the Swartland Revolution helped to set the industry on its ambitious trajectory. Rosa Kruger taught the country to recognize the treasure of its old-vine vineyards. But pioneers alone do not transform an industry. What turned their examples into a movement was the stubbornness, generosity, and ambition of an entire generation of winemakers, and, above all, their instinct to share knowledge rather than hoard it.

Ancient rocks and old vines may have given South Africa extraordinary raw materials, but its collaborative culture is what made the country’s wine so damn great, and what promises to keep it that way.

Tasting Notes

There are a lot of tasting notes below (more than 200), so here’s a handy link to jump to red wines if, for some silly reason, you want to skip all the world-class Chenin Blancs.

White Wines

White and Pink Wines With a Score Between 9.5 and 10

2018 Raats “Old Vine” Chenin Blanc, Polkadraai Hills, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of salty grapefruit and pear. In the mouth, wonderfully salty flavors of pear, Asian pear, white flowers, and candied grapefruit have a hint of wet pavement. Gorgeous, mouthwatering salinity. Fantastically delicious.13% alcohol. Cost: $34. click to buy.

2024 Mullineux “Straw Wine” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Medium yellow gold in the glass, this wine smells of honey, candied apricot, and white peaches. In the mouth, moderately sweet white peach and honey flavors have intensely bright, mouthwatering acidity, and a sensation of pure bright sunshine on the palate. Outstanding. Picked at normal ripeness and laid on racks to dry for 4 weeks. Takes 2 days to press and 12 months to ferment, stopping naturally. Very sweet. 7.5% alcohol. 345 g/l residual sugar. 375 ml bottle. Cost: $122. click to buy.

White and Pink Wines With a Score Around 9.5

2023 Cap Maritime Chardonnay, Upper Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Walker Bay, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon oil and white flowers. In the mouth, lemon pith and lemon oil flavors are wonderfully saline, with excellent acidity. Chalky, stony, and mouthwatering, with a lovely deep resonance to it. I couldn’t believe the price when I heard it. 13% alcohol. Cost: $19. click to buy.

2024 David & Nadia “Aristargos” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of apples, pears, and white flowers. In the mouth, lemon and pink grapefruit citrus oil and pith mix with pear, apple, and a hint of guava. Lean and bright, balanced and faintly saline with excellent acidity. Delicious. Whole-cluster pressed, fermented with ambient yeasts, then aged for 10 months in 20% concrete and the rest in old barrels. A blend of 51% Chenin Blanc, 13% Colombard, 11% Semillon, 10% Clairette, 8% Marsanne, 6% Roussanne, and 1% Grenache Blanc from 24 different picks across various vineyards and varieties. 13% alcohol. Cost: $36. click to buy.

2024 David & Nadia “Plat’bos” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest gold with hints of green, this wine smells of lemon oil and grapefruit pith. In the mouth, electric lemon and grapefruit oil flavors are brightly saline, lean, and mouthwatering. Salty lime, grapefruit, and lemon swirl with a hint of unripe pear. Grown on decomposed sandy granite and shale soils lacking clay. Plat’bos means “short plant.” 11.5% alcohol. Cost: $89. click to buy.

2024 David & Nadia “Langland” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear, pear skin, citrus pith, and white flowers. In the mouth, stony flavors of grapefruit pith, pear, and dried herbs have a juicy brightness thanks to excellent acidity. Saline and stony, with a faint chalky texture. Pure and crystalline in aspect. Langland means “long land.” Planted in 1971 on east-facing pure white granite sands in a valley with less light. 700 bottles made. 12.5% alcohol. Cost: $89.

2024 David & Nadia “Hoë-Steen” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light gold in the glass, this wine smells of pear, yellow plum, grapefruit pith, and wet chalkboard. In the mouth, silky, broad flavors of citrus oil, unripe pear, grapefruit, and dried herbs are shot through with a delicate wet chalkboard minerality. Saline and mouthwatering, but also smooth and silky. Grown on iron-rich clay over limestone on a southern slope. Whole-cluster pressed to tank, then fermented with solids in old barrels using ambient yeasts. Aged on gross lees for 10 months before bottling unfined and unfiltered. Hoë-Steen means “high stone.” 900 bottles made. 14% alcohol. Cost: $89. click to buy.

2022 Hamilton Russell “Ashbourne” Chardonnay, Hemel-en-Aarde, Walker Bay, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Palest gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon oil and bee pollen. In the mouth, lemon, green apple, bee pollen, and citrus pith flavors have lovely acidity and depth. A blend of Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, and Semillon, all amphora-fermented. Distinctive and compelling. 13% alcohol. Cost: $??

2024 Jordan “Timepiece” Sauvignon Blanc, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of passionfruit, white flowers, and honeydew. In the mouth, green apple, honeydew, and passionfruit flavors mix with salty lime zest and lime blossom. Fantastic acidity and deep stony minerality. From 1983 plantings. 13% alcohol. Cost: $??

2007 Ken Forrester “Old Vine Reserve” Chenin Blanc, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light greenish gold in the glass, this wine smells of butterscotch and salty candied apple. In the mouth, salty butterscotch, green apple, poached pear, and hints of yellow herbs are nicely mineral, salty, and delicious. Excellent acidity. Aging beautifully. Cost: $n/a

2021 Kumusha “The Flame Lily” Chenin Blanc, Slanghoek, Breedekloof, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest greenish gold, near colorless in the glass, this wine smells of white flowers, peach, and pear. In the mouth, faintly salty Asian pear, winter melon, white flowers, and a touch of pastry cream are all delicious. Excellent acidity. A blend of Chenin Blanc, Roussanne, Semillon, and Colombard. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $39. click to buy.

2017 Longridge “Clos du Ciel” Chardonnay, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of wet pavement and floral scents mixed with citrus oils. In the mouth, zippy grapefruit flavors mix with lemon and wet chalkboard, as sizzling acidity carries notes of dried herbs into the finish. Fantastically bright, persistent, and long. 12.5% alcohol. Cost: $??

2024 Mullineux “Old Vines White” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of pears, white flowers, yellow herbs, and apples. In the mouth, lemon peel and lemon pith mix with pink grapefruit, white flowers, vanilla, and poached pear. Bright, rich, and faintly saline, with a lovely wet pavement texture underneath. Delicious, with a hint of fynbos in the finish. A blend of 70% Chenin Blanc, with the balance made up of Clairette Blanche, Viognier, Grenache Blanc, and Semillon Gris from about seven Paardeberg granite sites. 13.5% alcohol. 3,137 cases made. Cost: $42. click to buy.

2024 Mullineux “Granite – Eikelaan Vineyard” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale yellow gold in the glass, this wine smells of bee pollen, chamomile, pear, and hints of struck match and wet pavement. In the mouth, pear, pear skin, wet pavement, hints of elderflower, citrus pith, and a touch of roasted nuts have a deeply crystalline aspect and wonderful faint salinity. Whole-cluster pressed, then fermented and aged in neutral oak for 11 months. Grown at 400 meters elevation. Eikelaan means “oak lane.” 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $93. click to buy.

2024 Mullineux “Iron – Rondomskirk” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Pale yellow gold in color, this wine smells of nectarine and pear, with hints of yellow flowers and bee pollen. In the mouth, electric lemon, lemon curd, and nectarine flavors mix with hints of pear and a broad silky texture. Faint wet pavement notes creep underneath, but this wine is a sunrise on the palate, intense and golden. Great acidity. Grown on reddish clay soils. Rondomskrik means “frightened from all around.” 591 cases made. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $103. click to buy.

2023 Mullineux “Roundstone Estate” White Blend, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light yellow-gold in the glass, this wine smells of crushed eggshells, white flowers, pears, and lemon oil. In the mouth, white nectarine, lemon oil, pear, and white flowers mix with zingy bright acidity and faint wet-pavement minerality. Faintly saline, wonderfully broad and rich, while at the same time maintaining a neon-lemon brightness. A hint of vanilla lingers in the finish, but there’s no new oak at work here. Whole-cluster pressed, fermented in old oak and some concrete egg. Aged for 11 months before bottling. A blend of equal parts Macabeo, Vermentino, Verdelho, Chenin Blanc, and Assyrtiko. 273 cases made. 13.5% alcohol. Cost: $62. click to buy.

NV Mullineux “Olerasay” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light amber in the glass, this wine smells of roasted nuts, honey, candied apricots, and butterscotch. In the mouth, butterscotch, honey, candied white peaches, and apricots are very sweet with excellent acidity. Silky and rich and weighty. Notes of butterscotch and a hint of coffee with milk linger in the finish. 365 g/l residual sugar. A solera of vintages from 2008 to 2024. 8% alcohol. Cost: $311. click to buy.

2021 Raats “Eden – High Density” Chenin Blanc, Polkedraai Hills, Stellenbosch, Coastal Region, South Africa
Palest greenish gold in color, this wine smells of wet pavement, pear, grapefruit, and citrus pith. In the mouth, wonderfully bright citrus, wet pavement, candied ginger, grapefruit pith, and grapefruit juice have a crystalline minerality. Gorgeously saline. Aged in 50% concrete egg and 50% oak (50% new). 8,000 vines per hectare. 13% alcohol. Cost: $81. click to buy.

2024 Storm Wines “Ridge” Chardonnay, Hemel-en-Aarde Ridge, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Pale gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon pith, wet chalkboard, and fynbos herbs. In the mouth, gorgeous saline flavors of lemon pith and grapefruit mix with wet chalkboard and green herbs. Silky and lean with excellent acidity and stony minerality. About 25% of the wine naturally failed to go through malolactic conversion. Aged for 11 months in 22% new oak, with 15% aged in clay amphora. 13.0% alcohol. Cost: $59. click to buy.

2024 Storm Wines “2025 CWG Auction Lot – Vrede” Chardonnay, Hemel-en-Aarde Valley, Cape South Coast, South Africa
Pale yellow-green gold in color, this wine smells of roasted nuts, lemon peel, and grapefruit pith. In the mouth, faintly saline flavors of lemon peel and lemon pith mix with unripe apple and wet chalkboard. A lightly grippy texture leaves a chalky sensation in the mouth. Aged in 30% new Louis Latour cooperage oak. 13.3% alcohol. Cost: $75. click to buy. (Note that link goes to the standard Vrede Chardonnay bottling, not the Cape Winemakers Guild wine, which was a special bottling).

2023 Van Loggerenberg “Kamaraderie” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light yellow gold in the glass, this wine smells of lemon-scented quartz and bee pollen. In the mouth, gorgeous silky-textured flavors of unripe pear, lemon oil, grapefruit pith, and crushed stones have gorgeous minerality and excellent acidity. Bottled, crystalline sunlight. From Lammershoek vines planted in 1966. Fermented and aged 85% in concrete tank and 15% in a 500-liter French oak barrel. 13% alcohol. Cost: $49. click to buy.

2024 Van Loggerenberg “Kamaraderie” Chenin Blanc, Swartland, Coastal Region, South Africa
Light yellow gold in color, this wine smells of pear, lemon oil, and bee pollen. In the mouth, salty lemon oil, pear, and white flower flavors have a brilliance like clear quartz crystal, with a hint of chopped green herbs. Stony minerality lingers in the finish with a lovely salinity and snap thanks to very good acidity. Aged 85% in concrete and 15% in a 500-liter old oak barrel. 13.2% alcohol. Cost: $49. click to buy.

2024 Wolf & Woman “Always Present Often Invisible” Chenin Blanc, Olifants River, South Africa

content:
Way out in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, the Azores Islands of Portugal host a remarkable and distinctive approach to viticulture. The grapevines are grown in cracks and fissures found or made in the solid volcanic lava beds that surround the island, and to protect the scraggly vines from the incessant winds, individual vines and small groups are surrounded by hand-built volcanic stone walls. Known as currais in Portuguese, these stacked-stone corrals are arranged in a zig-zag, maze-like fashion to avoid lengthy channels that can funnel winds between corrals. Consequently, it is impossible to walk through a vineyard in a straight line, and doing anything to an entire vineyard, such as pruning, picking, or treating the grapes takes an exceptional amount of time and effort.

content:
There aren’t many tastings in California where the wine trade lines up more than an hour in advance of the doors opening. But that’s precisely what happens ahead of the annual Oakville Winegrowers event in Napa Valley. Why? Because for many, myself included, this tasting is the sole opportunity each year to taste many of Napa’s most sought-after and exclusive wines. The Oakville AVA hosts a large percentage of the so-called cult wines of Napa Valley, including names such as Screaming Eagle, Dalla Valle, Harlan Estate, and BOND—and most of these are available for tasting at the event.

This year, the event returned to its customary home at the recently remodeled Robert Mondavi Winery. The space was lovely, though the combination of indoor and outdoor space suffered a bit in the heat of the day, making for a less than ideal tasting environment.

Despite the warmth, an enthusiastic crowd of buyers, consultants, sommeliers, and wine writers gathered to see what the 2022 and 2023 vintages looked like from this storied stretch of Napa Valley.

Personally, all other things being equal, I favor the generally cooler 2023 vintage when it comes to Napa Cabernet. However, many top producers in the valley made exceptional 2022 wines that don’t obviously show the much hotter qualities of that year.

The standout of the tasting, however, was the 2021 ULYSSES Red Wine that Christian Moueix makes from a 40-acre parcel that was once part of the Charles Hopper Ranch in Oakville. Mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with a bit of Cabernet Franc and a touch of Petit Verdot, it had incredible balance and complexity with a texture that was extremely beguiling. A proper pairing for the summer of the The Odyssey, and an incredible deal at $175 per bottle, if you can get ahold of one.

Looking up current prices for these wines on Wine-Searcher offers a sobering reminder of just how expensive Napa Valley Cabernet has become. I’m a serious and dedicated wine lover, but I very rarely pay more than $100 for a bottle of wine at retail. The top-scoring wines below average roughly $327 per bottle. That staggering figure puts them firmly out of reach for all but the wealthiest wine lovers. Many factors have contributed to the rising price of Napa Cabernet Sauvignon, but prices at this level increasingly turn wines into collectibles and markers of social capital rather than bottles to be opened and enjoyed. I think that’s a real shame.

Scores

Sometimes at large public tastings, I prefer to taste as widely as possible, and then simply score wines rather than trying to make coherent notes on 100+ bottles. Given the size of the tasting, the crush of people, as well as the heat, that’s the approach I decided to take at this event. Those who prefer wine evaluation done in more controlled conditions are welcome to take these scores with a grain of salt.

title: West Coast Aligoté Shines
summary:
Aligoté is having a moment. The workhorse white grape of Burgundy has spent much of the last half-century better known

The post West Coast Aligoté Shines appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Aligoté is having a moment. The workhorse white grape of Burgundy has spent much of the last half-century better known for kirs – cocktails made from dry white wine and crème de cassis – than fine wine. Today, it has become a darling of American wine connoisseurs.

As white burgundy prices have soared, Aligoté’s relatively modest cost, coupled with dramatic improvements in quality championed by dedicated advocates such as Sylvain Pataille and Aubert de Villaine, has fuelled an Aligoté renaissance, particularly in Bouzeron, the Burgundian village appellation specifically dedicated to the grape. These two producers, along with a band of Burgundians who call themselves Les Aligoteurs, have helped turn a grape valued as an occasional blending component or source of simple quaffing wine into a sought-after variety for serious white wines.

Not surprisingly, the rising star of Burgundian Aligoté has sparked producer interest in America. On 2 May, Balsall Creek winery in Oregon’s Willamette Valley held the Aligoté Affair, at which they and 11 other Oregon wineries poured their Aligotés for a sold-out crowd of 150. The event was billed as the first tasting dedicated to Aligoté in America. I couldn’t make it but the event did get me wondering just how many producers in Oregon and California were exploring the variety.

The answer? A lot more than I or anyone else expected.

title: Why South Africa Is the Most Exciting Wine Region on the Planet, Part II
summary:
This is Part II of a lengthy piece on South African wine. Read Part I here. In Part I, I

The post Why South Africa Is the Most Exciting Wine Region on the Planet, Part II appeared first on Vinography.
content:
This is Part II of a lengthy piece on South African wine. Read Part I here.

In Part I, I used the anarchic camaraderie of the Zoo Cru to illustrate something fundamental about South African wine: its unusual culture of collaboration. But collegiality alone cannot explain the country’s astonishing momentum. South Africa’s excitement comes from a convergence of ancient landscapes, old vineyards, stylistic relevance, brilliant hospitality, and a depth of winemaking talent that few regions can match.

Phenomenal Raw Materials

Those of us in the wine business often like to point out that the places where wine grows around the world are beautiful, which is true for the most part. But few bits of wine country can hold a candle to the sweeping beauty of South Africa.

Spectacular mountain vistas plunge toward the sea; craggy windswept highlands transform to lush protea-filled forests hosting troops of baboons; remote moonlike rocky plateaus can feel otherworldly. Some corners of the country feel nearly tropical while, elsewhere, stretches of bounteous farmland offer idyllic pastoral views.

The landscape of South Africa demands your attention and rewards your gaze at every turn. Anyone who comes over the pass into the valley of Franschhoek and fails to have their breath taken away should probably just be put out of their own misery.

Geologically speaking, a trip through the South African landscape represents an excursion into deep time. The country harbors some of the globe’s oldest, well-preserved exposed rocks and layers formed by sedimentary and volcanic activity, dating to more than 3.22 billion years ago.

Unlike some younger landscapes shaped primarily by tectonic uplift and volcanic eruptions, South Africa’s peaks, valleys, plains, and plateaus have largely been carved by billions of years of wind and water, punctuated by occasional cataclysms such as continental collisions and asteroid impacts. That geological complexity has left the Cape with an extraordinary mosaic of soils capable of supporting a wide range of grapevines.

South Africa’s wine country sits within a broadly Mediterranean climate, with warm, dry summers and cool, wet winters. But conditions vary tremendously throughout the Cape. Much of the Western Cape is cooled by the Atlantic Ocean and its icy Benguela Current, which generates fog and sends moisture-laden breezes into coastal vineyards during the growing season.

The country’s jagged mountains add even more variation. Elevation, slope, aspect, and distance from the sea can produce distinctly different mesoclimates within very short distances. Rainfall also varies dramatically, generally diminishing as you move north and inland, from relatively lush coastal and mountain sites to arid places where the survival of dry-farmed vineyards can seem almost miraculous. These climatic differences allow South Africa to ripen an enormous range of grape varieties. They have also helped produce an equally remarkable diversity of native plant life.

On top of South Africa’s stones and soil sits one of the world’s most diverse ecological zones, the Cape Floristic Region, sometimes known as the Cape Floral Kingdom. A combination of Mediterranean climate, infertile soils, recurrent wildfires, and wildly varying landscapes has contributed to the evolutionary isolation of the region. The resulting environment encouraged millions of years of what biologists call speciation, or the proliferation of new and different species from existing ones.

The Cape Floral Kingdom is the smallest of six floral kingdoms around the world, but the most diverse of them relative to its size. It hosts approximately 9,000 different plant species, of which more than 6,200 are found nowhere else on Earth. The characteristic vegetation of the kingdom is known as fynbos, a mix of dazzling floral plants such as protea and many other evergreen flowering shrubs, heaths, grasses, wildflowers, and succulents.

Walking through fynbos offers an experience as aromatic as it is visual. Like the characteristic garrigue of southeastern France, fynbos offers rich and unique smells including rooibos (which many people know from its popularity as a tisane), as well as other resinous and herbal aromas. Just as in Provence, these aromas can show up in the wines, sometimes hauntingly.

A Treasure Hiding in Plain Sight

One of the species that doesn’t naturally belong in this Cape Floral ecosystem is the wine grapevine, but Vitis vinifera has seemingly been quite comfortable in the nutrient-poor, rocky soils of the Cape since it arrived in 1655, carried and planted by Dutch settler Jan van Riebeeck.

His success in making the first wines in South Africa in 1659 encouraged farmers to plant vines wherever they saw fit to do so, and a particular set of economic and market realities ensured many of them stayed there.

South Africa, like some other sections of wine country around the world, possesses an incredible bounty of old vines, for many of the same reasons that Lodi in California still hosts a plethora of ancient Zinfandel.

The KWV Cooperative, soon after its launch in 1918, became the dominant force in the South African wine industry, eventually controlling the vast majority of its production with strict rules for growers. As a reliable customer to thousands of individual grape farmers throughout the country, KWV was counted on to purchase grapes for many decades. This steady, guaranteed income encouraged farmers to leave their vines in the ground and forgo the effort and expense of replanting or replacing them with other crops.

Later in the 20th century, when the wine market fell on hard times, it became simply too expensive to consider replanting them, or even ripping them out, so thousands of acres of mature vines, including precious scattered parcels approaching or exceeding a century in age, remained planted and in many cases producing. Today these vineyards are sought-after gems, prized by winemakers who understand the treasure that was hiding in plain sight.

South Africa owes its newfound appreciation for these old-vine resources largely to one person: Rosa Kruger. Kruger made early career stops in journalism and law before moving into agricultural management and viticulture in the late 1990s. In the early 2000s, inspired by visits to other regions around the world with old vines, she began to wonder what South Africa might have in the way of old vines. This led to years of driving around the country, discovering and documenting the country’s old vineyards.

In 2016, she formally established the Old Vine Project, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and ensuring the value of South Africa’s old-vine vineyards. What she has accomplished under the banner of this organization in a mere decade is astonishing.

Using planting records verified by South African Wine Industry Information and Systems (SAWIS), the Old Vine Project introduced its Certified Heritage Vineyard seal in 2018 for vineyards at least 35 years old. This first-of-its-kind program is designed to generate more revenue for the farmers of these old vines, and it’s working. Research suggests that South African consumers place a measurable premium on wines identified as coming from old vines.

The Old Vine Project has elevated and foregrounded the conversation about old vineyards and their value across culture, genetics, agronomy, history, and wine quality, as well as inspired many other old-vine initiatives around the world, including the Old Vine Registry.

Many Routes to Delicious

A great wine region offers more than compelling bottles. It also rewards wine lovers who make the journey to stand among its vines.

Wine tourism in South Africa has improved significantly in the past 20 years and now offers an impressive array of experiences for serious wine lovers as well as the merely wine-inclined world traveler. The Western Cape boasts more than 20 distinct wine regions, many with strong regional identities and well-established Wine Routes.

The Cape Town wine region puts wineries within easy reach of the cosmopolitan and lively city of the same name, making winery stops possible via taxi or rideshare, even down to rugged Cape Point, where crisp Sauvignon Blancs can be consumed oceanside with fresh seafood. Nearby Constantia offers beautiful historic estates with ocean views, while Stellenbosch surrounds a small town packed with restaurants, shops, and bars. The epicenter of Cabernet Sauvignon production in South Africa, Stellenbosch makes historic estates such as Kanonkop and Meerlust key pilgrimage stops for Cab lovers.

With a car, wine lovers can go farther afield. The cooler-climate Elgin Valley and Bot River regions make excellent Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc, Chenin Blanc, and increasingly interesting Rhône varieties. Farther along the coast, the windswept and craggy Hemel-en-Aarde Valley and Walker Bay countryside offer excellent Pinot Noir, stunning coastline, and some of the most consistent whale watching anywhere in the world.

Franschhoek offers stunning mountain landscapes, excellent wines, boutique hotels, and good restaurants. What the Swartland lacks in tourist infrastructure, it makes up for in sweeping vistas and spectacular wines, many of which come from old vines. More remote regions require slightly more planning, but readily welcome visitors, and increasing numbers of wineries offer guest accommodations, some of them quite luxurious.

South African wineries also offer some of the most impressive dining opportunities in the country. When the Michelin Guide gets to South Africa—not really a question of if, but when—mark my words, there will be more starred restaurants at wineries than in Cape Town itself. Many wineries now offer full-service dining, and a few of those kitchens are truly world-class.

There’s great food all over South Africa, with a strong focus on local sourcing, indigenous ingredients, and even foraging. Ocean bounty, wild game, excellent beef, and seasonal produce give local chefs plenty to work with. I have come to adore the country’s culinary variety, from casual braais to haute cuisine.

Beyond wine and food, South Africa offers mountain biking, surfing, hiking, paragliding, wildlife safaris, and the cosmopolitan vibrance of Cape Town. Combine all that with the quality and distinctiveness of the country’s wines, and South Africa easily vaults into the top tier of wine destinations around the world.

Beauty, hospitality, and a compelling travel experience alone do not make a great wine culture. Ultimately, the argument for South Africa being the world’s most exciting wine country rests on what ends up in the glass.

Fine Wines for Today’s Drinkers

Among the sommeliers, merchants, and engaged drinkers who shape conversations about wines over $25, the past 10 years have seen a growing appetite for freshness, moderate alcohol, less conspicuous oak, less-familiar grape varieties, and wines with strong regional identities.

South Africa’s current wine scene seems shockingly tailor-made for this moment. A whole generation of winemakers, informed by the pioneers of the Swartland Revolution, have adopted a lower-intervention approach to winemaking that, in addition to making thrilling wines, does an incredible job of showcasing South Africa’s varied terroir. The relative absence of new-oak signatures, combined with picking dates that preserve acidity and moderate ripeness, allows these wines to foreground site over cellar technique.

These winemakers have fully embraced the old-vine legacy of their homeland and now go to great lengths to ferret out patches of old vines and heritage grape varieties. South Africa is now making world-class Syrah, Cinsault, Grenache, Pinot Noir, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Palomino, Colombard, and of course, Chenin Blanc, in addition to stalwarts such as Cabernet Sauvignon, Chardonnay, and the uniquely local grape Pinotage. After years of a few producers making separate bottlings with the rosy-colored fruit that some of their Semillon vines occasionally produced, in 2026 the government recognized Semillon Gris as a legal variety, paving the way for another idiosyncratic South African winegrape rarely found elsewhere in the world.

When it comes to bubbles, South Africa has spent decades perfecting Cap Classique, its traditional-method sparkling wine. Made with the traditional Champagne grapes (Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, and Pinot Meunier) much of the time, the wine can also be made with Chenin Blanc, offering a particularly delicious take on the region’s signature white grape. Some Cap Classique producers have taken to very long lees aging, much like prestige Champagnes, and the results can be electrifying.

Pinotage represents perhaps the most stubbornly “local” grape variety found in South Africa. Developed in Stellenbosch in 1925 as a cross between Cinsault and Pinot Noir, it has long been considered the country’s signature red grape, but has struggled to win over many consumers. However, a newer approach to winemaking and site selection shows great promise, as I wrote about in my article Pinotage is Dead, Long Live Pinotage! earlier this year.

A discussion of South African wine styles would not be complete without the late-harvest sweet wines that made the country famous in the 18th and 19th centuries. Often made from Muscat, historically known as Hanepoot, these unfortified wines were once in high demand around the world. Today, wines such as Vin de Constance have revived the tradition in small but delicious quantities, combining vivid sweetness with enough acidity to stand alongside the world’s legendary dessert wines.

A New Homeland for Chenin

Chenin first came to South Africa in Jan van Riebeeck’s initial importation of grapevines in 1655 and was known locally as Steen for more than 300 years until 1963, when it was identified conclusively as Chenin Blanc.

Interestingly, some of the Chenin Blanc plant material that has been grown in South Africa for three centuries no longer exists in the Loire Valley. What’s more, recent research suggests that centuries of propagation under South African conditions have produced measurable epigenetic differences from Loire material, adding another dimension to the Cape’s distinctive expression of the grape.

I believe South Africa now rivals or even exceeds the grape’s homeland in the Loire Valley in producing extremely high-quality bottlings of this grape. That’s a bold statement, to be sure, but I confidently stand behind it. There are a few superstar producers of Chenin Blanc in the Loire that are unassailable, of course, but the Loire also makes plenty of mediocre Chenin. South Africa, on the other hand, can be distinguished not only by the heights of its greatest Chenins but also by the sheer breadth of excellence beneath them.

Talent at an Exceptional Scale

One of the most impressive things about South African wine right now is the sheer number of world-class independent wine producers making wine at the top of their game. In most wine regions around the world, only a small new wave of producers, often from a younger generation, defines the cutting edge of winemaking with exceptional wines. Think Chacra in Argentina; Comando G in Spain; or Kusuda in New Zealand. You get the idea.

South Africa doesn’t just have a handful of these producers; it has many dozens of such independent producers and labels in addition to the members of the Zoo Cru that I highlighted in Part I of this narrative. These are producers whose portfolios I can taste through, and after eight, ten, even fifteen wines, I haven’t encountered a single disappointing wine.

This isn’t normal for a region still considered up-and-coming in the world, especially not one that has only been developing in the modern sense since the end of apartheid in 1994. What South Africa has accomplished in the last three decades simply blows my mind.

Eben Sadie and the Swartland Revolution helped to set the industry on its ambitious trajectory. Rosa Kruger taught the country to recognize the treasure of its old-vine vineyards. But pioneers alone do not transform an industry. What turned their examples into a movement was the stubbornness, generosity, and ambition of an entire generation of winemakers, and, above all, their instinct to share knowledge rather than hoard it.

Ancient rocks and old vines may have given South Africa extraordinary raw materials, but its collaborative culture is what made the country’s wine so damn great, and what promises to keep it that way.

content:
Way out in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, the Azores Islands of Portugal host a remarkable and distinctive approach to viticulture. The grapevines are grown in cracks and fissures found or made in the solid volcanic lava beds that surround the island, and to protect the scraggly vines from the incessant winds, individual vines and small groups are surrounded by hand-built volcanic stone walls. Known as currais in Portuguese, these stacked-stone corrals are arranged in a zig-zag, maze-like fashion to avoid lengthy channels that can funnel winds between corrals. Consequently, it is impossible to walk through a vineyard in a straight line, and doing anything to an entire vineyard, such as pruning, picking, or treating the grapes takes an exceptional amount of time and effort.

content:
There aren’t many tastings in California where the wine trade lines up more than an hour in advance of the doors opening. But that’s precisely what happens ahead of the annual Oakville Winegrowers event in Napa Valley. Why? Because for many, myself included, this tasting is the sole opportunity each year to taste many of Napa’s most sought-after and exclusive wines. The Oakville AVA hosts a large percentage of the so-called cult wines of Napa Valley, including names such as Screaming Eagle, Dalla Valle, Harlan Estate, and BOND—and most of these are available for tasting at the event.

This year, the event returned to its customary home at the recently remodeled Robert Mondavi Winery. The space was lovely, though the combination of indoor and outdoor space suffered a bit in the heat of the day, making for a less than ideal tasting environment.

Despite the warmth, an enthusiastic crowd of buyers, consultants, sommeliers, and wine writers gathered to see what the 2022 and 2023 vintages looked like from this storied stretch of Napa Valley.

Personally, all other things being equal, I favor the generally cooler 2023 vintage when it comes to Napa Cabernet. However, many top producers in the valley made exceptional 2022 wines that don’t obviously show the much hotter qualities of that year.

The standout of the tasting, however, was the 2021 ULYSSES Red Wine that Christian Moueix makes from a 40-acre parcel that was once part of the Charles Hopper Ranch in Oakville. Mostly Cabernet Sauvignon with a bit of Cabernet Franc and a touch of Petit Verdot, it had incredible balance and complexity with a texture that was extremely beguiling. A proper pairing for the summer of the The Odyssey, and an incredible deal at $175 per bottle, if you can get ahold of one.

Looking up current prices for these wines on Wine-Searcher offers a sobering reminder of just how expensive Napa Valley Cabernet has become. I’m a serious and dedicated wine lover, but I very rarely pay more than $100 for a bottle of wine at retail. The top-scoring wines below average roughly $327 per bottle. That staggering figure puts them firmly out of reach for all but the wealthiest wine lovers. Many factors have contributed to the rising price of Napa Cabernet Sauvignon, but prices at this level increasingly turn wines into collectibles and markers of social capital rather than bottles to be opened and enjoyed. I think that’s a real shame.

Scores

Sometimes at large public tastings, I prefer to taste as widely as possible, and then simply score wines rather than trying to make coherent notes on 100+ bottles. Given the size of the tasting, the crush of people, as well as the heat, that’s the approach I decided to take at this event. Those who prefer wine evaluation done in more controlled conditions are welcome to take these scores with a grain of salt.

title: West Coast Aligoté Shines
summary:
Aligoté is having a moment. The workhorse white grape of Burgundy has spent much of the last half-century better known

The post West Coast Aligoté Shines appeared first on Vinography.
content:
Aligoté is having a moment. The workhorse white grape of Burgundy has spent much of the last half-century better known for kirs – cocktails made from dry white wine and crème de cassis – than fine wine. Today, it has become a darling of American wine connoisseurs.

As white burgundy prices have soared, Aligoté’s relatively modest cost, coupled with dramatic improvements in quality championed by dedicated advocates such as Sylvain Pataille and Aubert de Villaine, has fuelled an Aligoté renaissance, particularly in Bouzeron, the Burgundian village appellation specifically dedicated to the grape. These two producers, along with a band of Burgundians who call themselves Les Aligoteurs, have helped turn a grape valued as an occasional blending component or source of simple quaffing wine into a sought-after variety for serious white wines.

Not surprisingly, the rising star of Burgundian Aligoté has sparked producer interest in America. On 2 May, Balsall Creek winery in Oregon’s Willamette Valley held the Aligoté Affair, at which they and 11 other Oregon wineries poured their Aligotés for a sold-out crowd of 150. The event was billed as the first tasting dedicated to Aligoté in America. I couldn’t make it but the event did get me wondering just how many producers in Oregon and California were exploring the variety.

The answer? A lot more than I or anyone else expected.
